{{Short description|Periodic minimal surface}}
In [[differential geometry]], the '''Schwarz minimal surfaces''' are [[Triply periodic minimal surface|periodic]] [[minimal surface]]s originally described by [[Hermann Schwarz]].

In the 1880s Schwarz and his student E.&nbsp;R.&nbsp;Neovius described periodic minimal surfaces.<ref>H. A. Schwarz, Gesammelte Mathematische Abhandlungen, Springer, Berlin, 1933.</ref><ref>E. R. Neovius, "Bestimmung zweier spezieller periodischer Minimalflächen", ''Akad. Abhandlungen'', Helsingfors, 1883.</ref> They were later named by [[Alan Schoen]] in his seminal report that described the [[gyroid]] and other triply periodic minimal surfaces.<ref>Alan H. Schoen, Infinite periodic minimal surfaces without self-intersections, NASA Technical Note TN D-5541 (1970)[https://ntrs.nasa.gov/archive/nasa/casi.ntrs.nasa.gov/19700020472.pdf]</ref>

The surfaces were generated using symmetry arguments: given a solution to [[Plateau's problem]] for a polygon, reflections of the surface across the boundary lines also produce valid minimal surfaces that can be continuously joined to the original solution. If a minimal surface meets a plane at right angles, then the mirror image in the plane can also be joined to the surface. Hence given a suitable initial polygon inscribed in a unit cell periodic surfaces can be constructed.<ref>Hermann Karcher, Konrad Polthier, "Construction of Triply Periodic Minimal Surfaces", ''Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. A'' 16 September 1996 vol. 354 no. 1715 2077–2104</ref>

The Schwarz surfaces have [[Genus (mathematics)|topological genus]] 3, the minimal genus of triply periodic minimal surfaces.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://schoengeometry.com/e-tpms.html|title = Alan Schoen geometry}}</ref>

They have been considered as models for periodic [[nanostructures]] in [[block copolymer]]s, electrostatic equipotential surfaces in crystals,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mackay |first1=Alan L. |title=Periodic minimal surfaces |journal=Nature |date=April 1985 |volume=314 |issue=6012 |pages=604–606 |doi=10.1038/314604a0|bibcode=1985Natur.314..604M |s2cid=4267918 }}</ref> and hypothetical negatively curved graphite phases.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Terrones |first1=H. |last2=Mackay |first2=A. L. |title=Negatively curved graphite and triply periodic minimal surfaces |journal=Journal of Mathematical Chemistry |date=December 1994 |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=183–195 |doi=10.1007/BF01277558|s2cid=123561096 }}</ref>

== Schwarz P ("Primitive") ==
[[File:Schwarz P Surface.png|thumb|Schwarz P surface]]

Schoen named this surface 'primitive' because it has two intertwined congruent labyrinths, each with the shape of an inflated tubular version of the simple cubic lattice. While the standard P surface has cubic symmetry the unit cell can be any rectangular box, producing a family of minimal surfaces with the same topology.<ref>W. H. Meeks. The theory of triply-periodic minimal surfaces. Indiana University Math. Journal, 39 (3):877-936, 1990.</ref>

It can be approximated by the implicit surface
:<math> \cos(x) + \cos(y) + \cos(z) = 0 \ </math>.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.msri.org/publications/sgp/jim/geom/level/library/triper/index.html |title=Triply Periodic Level Surfaces |accessdate=2019-02-10 |url-status = live |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20190212011124/http://www.msri.org/publications/sgp/jim/geom/level/library/triper/index.html |archivedate=2019-02-12 }}</ref>

The P surface has been considered for prototyping [[tissue engineering|tissue scaffolds]] with a high surface-to-volume ratio and porosity.<ref>Jaemin Shin, Sungki Kim, Darae Jeong, Hyun Geun Lee, Dongsun Lee, Joong Yeon Lim, and Junseok Kim, Finite Element Analysis of Schwarz P Surface Pore Geometries for Tissue-Engineered Scaffolds, Mathematical Problems in Engineering, Volume 2012, Article ID 694194, doi:10.1155/2012/694194</ref>
{{clear}}

== Schwarz D ("Diamond") ==
[[File:Schwarz D Surface.png|thumb|Schwarz D surface]]
Schoen named this surface 'diamond' because it has two intertwined congruent labyrinths, each having the shape of an inflated tubular version of the [[Diamond lattice|diamond bond structure]]. It is sometimes called the F surface in the literature.

It can be approximated by the implicit surface

: <math>\cos(x)\cos(y)\cos(z) - \sin(x)\sin(y)\sin(z) = 0\ </math>.

Some sources give the alternate implicit surface

: <math>\sin(x)\sin(y)\sin(z) + \sin(x)\cos(y)\cos(z) + \cos(x)\sin(y)\cos(z) + \cos(x)\cos(y)\sin(z) = 0</math>

which is equivalent up to a translation in all coordinates by <math>\frac{\pi}{4}</math>.

An exact expression exists in terms of [[elliptic integrals]], based on the [[Weierstrass representation]].<ref>Paul J.F. Gandy, Djurdje Cvijović, Alan L. Mackay, Jacek Klinowski, Exact computation of the triply periodic D (`diamond') minimal surface, Chemical Physics Letters, Volume 314, Issues 5–6, 10 December 1999, Pages 543–551</ref>

{{clear}}

== Schwarz H ("Hexagonal") ==
[[File:Schwarz H Surface.png|thumb|Schwarz H surface]]
The H surface is similar to a [[catenoid]] with a triangular boundary, allowing it to tile space.

{{clear}}
